questions.q: Which chemical elements make up carbohydrates and lipids?
What are proteins principally composed of in terms of chemical elements?
a: Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen (and sometimes sulfur)

questions.q: What are the smaller basic units (monomers) that join together to form complex starch and glycogen carbohydrates?
What are the building blocks of protein molecules?
Which of the following describes the basic structure of a triglyceride lipid molecule?
a: One glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acid chains
A long chain of glucose monomers
A central nitrogen atom bonded to carbon

questions.q: What is the chemical test used to test for the presence of reducing sugars (such as glucose), and what is a positive color change?
a: Iodine test; changes from brown to blue-black
Benedict's test with heating; changes from blue to green, yellow, orange, or brick-red
Biuret test; changes from blue to purple
Ethanol emulsion test; forms a milky white emulsion

questions.q: Which chemical test is used to detect starch, and what is a positive result?
a: Iodine solution test; changes from yellowish-brown to blue-black

questions.q: What is the name of the chemical test used to detect proteins, and what color indicates a positive result?
a: Biuret test (using copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide); changes from blue to purple/violet

questions.q: How is the ethanol emulsion test performed to test for lipids (fats)?
a: Mix the sample with ethanol, shake thoroughly, then pour the mixture into water; a cloudy white emulsion indicates lipids
Heat the sample with Benedict's solution
Add iodine solution directly to dry powder
Dissolve the sample in acid and check for gas bubbles

questions.q: What is an enzyme defined as in biological systems?
a: A high-energy molecule used for cellular respiration
A biological catalyst made of protein that speeds up specific chemical reactions without being used up itself
A structural component of cell walls
A hormone that regulates blood sugar

questions.q: What is the specific region on an enzyme molecule where the substrate binds during a biochemical reaction?
How does the 'lock and key' hypothesis explain enzyme specificity?
a: Enzymes change their shape to fit any substrate randomly
Enzymes act as physical locks that destroy substrates permanently
The shape of the active site of a specific enzyme is complementary to the shape of its specific substrate, fitting together like a key in a lock
Enzymes use keys to unlock cell membranes

questions.q: What happens to the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction as temperature increases from low up to the optimum temperature?
a: The rate increases because thermal energy increases the kinetic energy and frequency of successful collisions between enzyme and substrate
The rate decreases immediately because enzymes freeze
Enzymes are permanently destroyed at low temperatures

questions.q: What occurs when an enzyme is subjected to temperatures significantly higher than its optimum (e.g., above 60°C)?
a: The enzyme works twice as fast permanently
The enzyme's active site changes shape (denatures), meaning the substrate can no longer bind and the reaction stops
The enzyme turns into a lipid

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'optimum pH' for an enzyme?
a: The pH level where the enzyme is completely destroyed
The pH where the enzyme stops working entirely
The pH value at which an enzyme exhibits its highest rate of activity
The pH level found exclusively in plant roots

questions.q: How does extreme pH (very high acidity or alkalinity) affect enzyme activity?
a: It turns substrate molecules into proteins
It improves the fit of the active site
It alters the charge and structure of the enzyme, denaturing the active site and stopping the reaction

questions.q: Why are enzymes described as biological catalysts that remain unchanged at the end of a reaction?
a: They participate in the reaction to lower activation energy and form products, but are released unchanged and can catalyze further reactions
They are consumed and destroyed during the reaction

questions.q: Which of the following biological molecules functions as an important long-term energy store and provides thermal insulation in animals?
What is the primary function of DNA as a biological molecule?
a: To act as a catalyst for digestion
To provide immediate energy for muscle contraction
To store genetic information that codes for proteins and controls inherited characteristics
To transport oxygen in the blood

questions.q: Which of the following elements is found in proteins and nucleic acids, but is typically absent in carbohydrates and lipids?
What role do water molecules play as a solvent within living organisms?
a: Water acts as an excellent medium for metabolic chemical reactions and transport, dissolving many polar and ionic substances
Water acts as a primary enzyme catalyst

questions.q: If an enzyme has an optimum temperature of 37°C, what would happen to its activity if placed in an environment at 0°C?
a: The enzyme is permanently denatured and destroyed
Activity drops to near zero because molecules have very low kinetic energy, but the enzyme is not permanently denatured
The enzyme converts into a substrate

questions.q: What is activation energy, and how do enzymes affect it?
a: The energy required to destroy an enzyme; enzymes increase it
The energy stored in products; enzymes keep it constant
The minimum energy required to start a chemical reaction; enzymes lower activation energy, speeding up the reaction
The kinetic energy of water; enzymes remove it

questions.q: Which of the following correctly pairs a food molecule with its primary chemical building blocks?
What term describes the complex formed temporarily when an enzyme binds to its specific substrate during a reaction?
Why does boiling an enzyme solution permanently destroy its catalytic activity?
a: Because high heat increases kinetic energy
Because high temperatures break chemical bonds holding the enzyme's 3D tertiary structure, permanently altering the shape of the active site (denaturation)
Because boiling turns the enzyme into water

questions.q: Which macromolecule category includes cellulose, starch, and glycogen?
What happens to the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction when substrate concentration is increased while enzyme concentration remains constant?
a: The rate increases and then reaches a maximum point (saturation) where all active sites are occupied

questions.q: What is the main difference between monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides?
a: The number of sugar monomer units linked together (single units, double units, or many units)
The presence of nitrogen in polysaccharides
Whether they contain lipids or proteins

questions.q: Which enzyme breaks down starch into simpler sugars (maltose)?
What are the products formed when lipase enzymes digest lipid molecules?
Which enzyme group is responsible for breaking down proteins into amino acids?
Why do different enzymes in the human body (such as pepsin in the stomach versus trypsin in the small intestine) have very different optimum pH levels?
a: Because pepsin functions in the highly acidic environment of the stomach (pH 2), whereas trypsin operates in the alkaline environment of the small intestine (pH 8)
Because stomach enzymes are made of lipids instead of proteins
Because pepsin digests starch while trypsin digests fat
Because pH has no effect on human enzymes

questions.q: What is the role of iodine solution in biological testing?
a: Testing for the presence of starch, changing from orange-brown to blue-black

questions.q: Which of the following substances is tested using the Biuret reagent?
What is the function of rough endoplasmic reticulum in relation to biological molecules?
a: To transport and process proteins synthesized by attached ribosomes

questions.q: Which chemical test requires heating the sample in a water bath with a specific blue reagent that turns brick-red if a high concentration of sugar is present?
Why is water considered an essential biological molecule for living organisms?
a: It provides high amounts of metabolic energy
It acts as a solvent for chemical reactions, a transport medium, and a reactant in digestion
It acts as an organic enzyme catalyst

questions.q: Which property of enzymes makes them extremely efficient in living cells?
a: They can only be used once
They require high temperatures to function
They are specific to one reaction or type of reaction and can work at very high turnover rates without being consumed
They convert all food into starch
